title: The Anti-Taliban Resistance Has Survived. Can It Win?
gist: Will Selber argues that Afghanistan's fragmented anti-Taliban resistance (over a dozen groups led by Massoud, Zia, Sadat and others) has survived five years without a state sponsor or sanctuary and is increasing its attack tempo, but has yet to hold any district. He urges the groups to unify under a Peshawar Seven-style umbrella and focus on seizing territory in Badakhshan, and recommends the West tacitly back Pakistan's emerging engagement with the resistance to preserve options as Islamabad-Taliban relations deteriorate.

insights.claim: Despite much-reported rivalry between Interior Minister Sirajuddin Haqqani and Supreme Leader Hibatullah Akhunzada, the Taliban has remained a unified front against its enemies.
insights.speaker: Will Selber
insights.so_what: Don't bet on internal Taliban fracture as a near-term regime-change catalyst.
insights.quote: for all the supposed infighting inside the Taliban, they have remained a unified front against its enemies

insights.claim: The anti-Taliban resistance, over a dozen groups led by former government leaders, has survived without a cross-border sanctuary or overt state sponsor, and over the last two years has multiplied and expanded the tempo and geographic reach of its attacks.
insights.speaker: Will Selber
insights.so_what: Low-level insurgency is growing and could raise security risk in northern and southern Afghanistan.
insights.quote: In the last two years, these groups have multiplied, and the tempo and geographical reach of their attacks have expanded.

insights.claim: U.N. reports document at least 438 verified resistance attacks and incidents between November 2023 and July 2026, which resistance leaders say is an undercount.
insights.speaker: Will Selber
insights.so_what: Verified data confirm the insurgency is real, not a social-media artifact.
insights.quote: A tally of verified attacks and incidents documented in successive U.N. reports establishes a minimum of 438
insights.locator: The anti-Taliban resistance groups regularly claim

insights.claim: Lt. Gen. Sami Sadat's Afghan United Front began combat operations on Aug. 1, 2026 and claimed over 60 guerrilla attacks through September, focusing on southern Afghanistan, the Taliban's spiritual heartland; Sadat has ties to the Republican Party.
insights.speaker: Will Selber
insights.so_what: A Republican-linked resistance leader could gain traction in U.S. policy debates.

insights.claim: Yasin Zia's Afghanistan Freedom Front has struck in Pashtun areas including Kandahar and Helmand, suggesting wider operational reach than Ahmad Massoud's Panjshir-focused National Resistance Front.
insights.speaker: Will Selber
insights.so_what: Resistance activity is spreading beyond traditional Tajik strongholds.

insights.claim: Resistance attacks have not translated into an existential challenge to Taliban control and no group has secured lasting control of any district.
insights.speaker: Will Selber
insights.so_what: Regime change in Afghanistan remains a low-probability scenario.
insights.quote: these attacks have yet to translate into an existential challenge to Taliban control

themes.theme: Fragmentation and the Peshawar Seven model

insights.claim: Fragmentation prevents resistance groups from pooling scarce resources and manpower and echoes the infighting that crippled the previous Afghan government.
insights.speaker: Will Selber
insights.so_what: Unity is the key variable to watch for any escalation of the insurgency.

insights.claim: The resistance should form an umbrella organization like the Soviet-era Peshawar Seven, with a power-sharing shura, inclusion of broader ethnic and religious communities, a common foreign-aid mechanism, and possibly a government in exile.
insights.speaker: Will Selber
insights.so_what: Formation of an umbrella body would be a signal of a more credible insurgency.

insights.claim: The Peshawar Seven channeled foreign aid via Pakistan's ISI, Operation Cyclone and Saudi support but did not end bloody factional rivalry, with patrons backing rival factions and Hekmatyar's forces killing 30 Massoud fighters in 1989.
insights.speaker: Will Selber
insights.so_what: Historical precedent warns that foreign-backed insurgency can lead to civil war.

insights.claim: On July 17, 2026, the Homeland Soldiers Front briefly captured the Yaftali Sufla district center in Badakhshan, a rare temporary loss of a district center for the Taliban since 2021.
insights.speaker: Will Selber
insights.so_what: Early indicator that territorial control could become contested in the northeast.

insights.claim: Badakhshan is the most attractive place for the resistance to seize territory due to remote mountainous terrain, a long resistance tradition, local grievances over Taliban restrictions on mining, and intra-Taliban clashes over gold mines.
insights.speaker: Will Selber
insights.so_what: Badakhshan mining areas are at elevated conflict risk.
insights.quote: The Taliban has also alienated local miners by restricting their livelihoods while allowing connected operators to profit.
insights.locator: Badakhshan also has a long resistance

insights.claim: The Taliban will find it harder to crush resistance in Badakhshan than in Panjshir in 2021 because the resistance now has five years of experience, the Taliban lacks its post-victory momentum, and it has failed to force groups like the Afghanistan Freedom Front to surrender.
insights.speaker: Will Selber
insights.so_what: Insurgency in the northeast could prove persistent.

insights.claim: Badakhshan borders Tajikistan, Pakistan and, via the Wakhan Corridor, China, whose pragmatic ties with the Taliban could shift if the Taliban keeps ignoring Beijing's requests to act against the East Turkestan Islamic Movement.
insights.speaker: Will Selber
insights.so_what: China-Taliban relations, relevant to Chinese mining and infrastructure bets in Afghanistan, hinge on militant control.

insights.claim: Pakistan's relations with the Taliban have deteriorated over Taliban support for the Pakistani Taliban and Ittihad al-Mujahideen Pakistan, leading to Pakistan's declaration of 'open war' on the Taliban.
insights.speaker: Will Selber
insights.so_what: Pakistan-Afghanistan conflict is a live regional risk affecting Pakistani security and trade.
insights.locator: However, since the fall of Kabul

insights.claim: The New York Times reported Pakistani military and intelligence officials have met resistance leaders to discuss potential support, which resistance groups privately call their only tangible option to gain traction.
insights.speaker: Will Selber
insights.so_what: Pakistan could become the resistance's sponsor, escalating proxy conflict.

insights.claim: Tajikistan is a plausible tacit supporter of the resistance but, given Russia's deepening engagement with the Taliban, is unlikely to provide more than passive assistance.
insights.speaker: Will Selber
insights.so_what: Russia's influence limits Central Asian backing for anti-Taliban forces.

insights.claim: Iran may offer diplomatic openings to the resistance given Massoud's invitation to Ali Khamenei's funeral and Tehran's concerns over eastern water rights and Taliban persecution of Shiites.
insights.speaker: Will Selber
insights.so_what: Iran-Taliban water disputes are a potential flashpoint.

insights.claim: The West should tacitly support Pakistan's engagement with the resistance at little cost to preserve options, and consider public support and resources if the groups unify and can seize and hold territory, since the Taliban's ability to constrain al-Qaeda is not indefinite.
insights.speaker: Will Selber
insights.so_what: A possible shift in U.S. Afghanistan policy that could renew proxy conflict.
